title: Embeddings & Vector Search

character.name: The Librarian
character.tagline: I don't file books by title. I file them by what they're ABOUT.

oneLiner: Turning meaning into numbers so machines can find things by concept, not just keywords.
analogy: Imagine a magical library where every book floats in space, and books about similar ideas drift close together — cookbooks huddle in one corner, space operas in another. That's an embedding space: each piece of text becomes a point (a vector), and nearness means similar meaning. To find relevant books you don't scan titles for exact words; you drop your question into the space and grab whatever's floating nearby. A vector database is the shelving system that makes finding those nearest neighbors fast, even among millions of books.
objectives: Understand embeddings as vectors capturing semantic meaning.
See how similarity (cosine distance) enables semantic search.
Know what a vector database does and when you need one.
Contrast semantic search with keyword search.
keyConcepts: An embedding maps text (or images, etc.) to a vector so that similar meanings are close together in vector space.
Semantic search compares embedding vectors (via cosine similarity) to find conceptually related items, even without shared keywords.
Vector databases (e.g. Pinecone, pgvector, FAISS) store embeddings and perform fast nearest-neighbor search at scale.
Embeddings power search, recommendations, clustering, deduplication, and the retrieval step in RAG.
Keyword search matches exact words; semantic search matches meaning — often you combine both (hybrid search).
Chunk size and the embedding model choice significantly affect retrieval quality.

keyTerms.plain: Meaning turned into a list of numbers (a point in concept-space).
A map where similar things sit close together.
A score for how close two meanings are.
A search engine for 'find me the nearest meanings, fast.'
Searching by idea, not exact words.

resources.label: Pinecone: What is a vector database?

scenarios.scenario: A help center search fails when users phrase questions differently from the article titles (e.g. 'my card was declined' vs 'payment failure').
scenarios.question: Which approach best fixes this?

options.label: Semantic search over embeddings, so conceptually similar phrasings match

scenarios.explanation: Embeddings capture meaning, so 'card declined' and 'payment failure' land near each other in vector space and match — something exact-keyword search misses.

quiz.question: An embedding is:
options: A vector of numbers representing the meaning of text (or other data)
A type of database index only
quiz.answer: A vector of numbers representing the meaning of text (or other data)
quiz.explanation: Embeddings encode semantic meaning as vectors so that similar items are close together in vector space.

quiz.question: How does semantic search decide what's relevant?
options: By measuring vector similarity (e.g. cosine) between query and item embeddings
quiz.answer: By measuring vector similarity (e.g. cosine) between query and item embeddings
quiz.explanation: It embeds the query and compares it to stored embeddings, returning the nearest (most similar in meaning) items.

quiz.question: What does a vector database specialize in?
options: Storing relational tables with SQL joins
Fast nearest-neighbor search over many embedding vectors
quiz.answer: Fast nearest-neighbor search over many embedding vectors
quiz.explanation: Vector DBs index embeddings for efficient similarity search at scale — the retrieval backbone for semantic search and RAG.

quiz.question: A key difference between keyword and semantic search is:
options: Keyword search understands meaning; semantic doesn't
Semantic search matches meaning even without shared exact words
Semantic search only works on numbers
quiz.answer: Semantic search matches meaning even without shared exact words
quiz.explanation: Keyword search needs matching terms; semantic search matches concepts. Hybrid approaches often combine both.

quiz.question: Embeddings are commonly used for all of these EXCEPT:
quiz.explanation: Embeddings enable search, recommendations, clustering, and RAG retrieval — they are not an encryption mechanism.
